name: Omar Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that doesn't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Pete and Anne Draper. They've got six thousand free-range laying hens in two big sheds, and about three hundred acres of wheat and oilseed rape. My mornings are the hens: walking the sheds, collecting floor eggs the hens lay in the wrong place, checking the drinkers, clearing out any dead birds. Afternoons it's the egg room, grading and packing, or helping Pete on the land when he needs a second pair of hands.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drove a bakery delivery van for nine years, then they merged two routes and I was the one left over. Pete's wife Anne knew Mei from the school office, where Mei works, and they needed someone. Three years in, I'm still slower in the egg room than Anne, and I've never driven the combine. We've got Jia, who's fifteen, and Sami, who's eleven, a mortgage, and maybe three weeks of money if things stopped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool and that's it. I use it now and then to tidy up an email to the feed company, and it's handy, but it's not running the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Means I carry on. Honestly, I'd be glad to be bored for a while. After losing the van job, I don't need anything else exciting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going at the Drapers', and ask Pete if I can start learning the combine this harvest. Keep using the AI for the odd letter. Try to get a little extra saved before Jia's school trip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit relieved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the combine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the egg room is where I'm slowest and it's the job most likely to get a machine anyway. If I can drive the big kit, Pete needs me for more of the year. It's just sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the school trip?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jia's class is going to the mountains for a week in spring, it's about three hundred. We'll find it. We always find it, it's just whatever else doesn't get done that month.

S0.say: He'd say AI is a useful tool and nothing more. He uses it now and then to tidy emails to the feed company, but it isn't running the farm.
S0.think: Privately he'd be glad of a quiet stretch after losing his delivery job. A plateau means he simply carries on.
S0.do: Keeps working at the egg and arable farm and asks to learn the combine this harvest. Keeps using AI for the odd letter and saves towards his daughter's school trip.
S0.quote: Honestly, I'd be glad to be bored for a while.
S0.fieldNote: Even with nothing changing, he's already thinking about which tasks are most exposed and moving towards the combine. Practical rather than political. His earlier job loss makes him value quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening, so let's be sensible and adjust. I'm not going to be the one moaning about it at the pub, there's no point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the egg room goes first. There are already machines that grade and pack faster than Anne, and robots that roll round the shed picking floor eggs. That's half my day, gone, and I'm the junior, so it's my hours that get cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Pete early and ask him to teach me the arable side properly, sprayer, combine, the lot. I'd learn the farm software, start using the AI more for the records so I'm useful in the office. And we'd start putting fifty a month away, even if it means no takeaway at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, but I'd feel it in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You lost a job when two routes merged. Does this feel like that again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. That time I saw it coming for six months and did nothing, I just hoped. I'm not doing the hoping thing again, I'm doing the asking-early thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Mei think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mei's calmer than me. She says the school will always need someone in the office, and she's probably right. Her job is the steady one, which is a strange thing to say about a school office.

S1.say: He'd say the change is happening and people should adjust sensibly. He wouldn't complain at the pub because he sees no point.
S1.think: Privately he expects egg grading and floor-egg collection to be automated first, which is half his day. As the junior, he expects his hours to be cut.
S1.do: Asks his employer early to teach him the arable work, from sprayer to combine, and learns the farm software. Uses AI more for records and starts saving fifty a month by dropping takeaways.
S1.feel: Anxious, a feeling in his stomach, but not panicked.
S1.quote: I'm not doing the hoping thing again, I'm doing the asking-early thing.
S1.fieldNote: He has learned from his last job loss and refuses to just hope. His partner's school job is the household's anchor. He reads steady disruption precisely in terms of his own tasks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need governments and companies to slow it down and look after people while it settles. I'm not left or right on it, I just think somebody has to be the grown-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think there's no job at the Drapers' in two years. If a robot can drive the combine and grade eggs, Pete won't keep me, he can't afford to. And driving's gone too, so I can't even go back to the van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look for any job with people in it straight away, the school caretaker job, a care home, anything local. I'd cut everything that's not the mortgage and food. And I'd apply for whatever support the government put up, without being shy about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Proper scared. I'd hide it from the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hide it. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me being cheerful at dinner and then sitting in the car in the drive for ten minutes. I did that for a month after the bakery job. Mei knew. The kids didn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does having only two years change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The plan in the slower picture was to learn the arable side and become harder to replace. With two years, the arable side goes as fast as the egg room. So there's nothing to learn into, I'd just be looking for any door that's still open.

S2.say: He'd call for governments and companies to slow things down and look after people while it settles. He sees it as a question of someone acting like the grown-up, not left or right.
S2.think: Privately he expects no job at the farm within two years, since robots could do both eggs and combine. Driving would be gone too, so he couldn't return to his old work.
S2.do: Applies straight away for any local job involving people, such as school caretaker or care home work. Cuts everything except mortgage and food, and applies for government support without shame.
S2.feel: Properly scared, hiding it from the children.
S2.quote: I did that for a month after the bakery job. Mei knew. The kids didn't.
S2.fieldNote: His careful plan from steady change collapses because arable work goes as fast as the egg room. He has a clear memory of hiding fear after his last job loss. Still pragmatic: looks for any door with people behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people stop arguing and plan. I'd tell people at work to start thinking now, not in year four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years gives me three or four more at the Drapers', which matters. It's enough to get Jia through school and into whatever comes next. It's not enough for me to become something new, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep learning the farm machines and the AI, so I'm useful longer. I'd ask Mei to keep an eye out for the caretaker job at her school, and apply the moment it's free. We'd change Jia's plans a bit, steer her towards nursing or something hands-on with people rather than accounting, which she's been talking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd have a plan, so I'd sleep most nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Jia accept being steered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, she's fifteen. But I'd show her the numbers, and she listens to numbers more than to me. She told me accounting was safe. I told her the AI already does my tax better than the accountant did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the difference between five years and two, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me jump from a moving boat instead of a sinking one. Two years, I'm in the water. It's the difference between choosing the caretaker job and grabbing anything.

S3.say: He'd say five years is enough to get ready if people stop arguing and plan. He'd tell co-workers to start thinking now, not in the last year.
S3.think: Privately five years gives him three or four more years at the farm and gets his daughter through school. It isn't enough for him to become something new.
S3.do: Keeps learning farm machinery and AI to stay useful longer and applies for the caretaker job at his partner's school when it opens. Steers his daughter towards nursing or hands-on people work instead of accounting.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with a plan, so he sleeps most nights.
S3.quote: She told me accounting was safe. I told her the AI already does my tax better than the accountant did.
S3.fieldNote: He frames the middle timeline as jumping from a moving boat rather than a sinking one. Family plans shift, with his daughter's career steered away from desk work. His steadiness shows in waiting for a specific, known job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair run-up and we'd be daft not to use it. I'd say the same thing at work and at home: start small, start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is fine for me. I'd be fifty-three and probably on my second job by then, maybe the caretaker one. The kids would be grown, and that's the part I care about most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a couple of years to see who's using what on other farms, then learn whatever the Drapers bring in. I'd keep the fifty a month going and try to pay a bit extra on the mortgage. I'd look at a caretaker or maintenance course around year five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the back of my mind, but I'd feel normal most days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you wouldn't do the hoping thing again. Isn't waiting two years a bit like hoping?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. It's different, I think, because I'd be watching on purpose, not ignoring it. Hoping is shutting your eyes. Waiting is keeping them open and your hand on the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sami, who's eleven?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That he'll be twenty-one when it lands and he should learn to fix things and talk to people. Sami's the chatty one, he'd be fine with people. I'd tell him not to bother being a delivery driver like his dad.

S4.say: He'd call ten years a fair run-up that should be used. At work and at home he'd say start small and start now.
S4.think: Privately ten years seems fine to him, as he'd be fifty-three and likely in a second job. What matters most is his children being grown.
S4.do: Waits a couple of years to see what other farms adopt, then learns whatever his employer brings in. Keeps saving fifty a month, pays extra on the mortgage and takes a caretaker or maintenance course around year five.
S4.feel: A little uneasy at the back of his mind, but normal most days.
S4.quote: Hoping is shutting your eyes. Waiting is keeping them open and your hand on the door.
S4.fieldNote: When challenged on waiting, he draws a clear line between watching on purpose and hoping. Typical steady adopter: lets others go first, then follows. His advice to his son centres on fixing things and people skills.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's nothing to step onto. What would help is support that doesn't make you feel like a beggar, and local jobs with people in them, care, schools, maintenance, kept going on purpose.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what it's like to lose a job and start again at forty. Starting at the bottom at forty isn't brave, it's just what you do when the van's gone. I'd do it again, I'd just like more warning.

headlineQuote: Starting at the bottom at forty isn't brave, it's just what you do when the van's gone.
portrait: Omar Zhang is a 43-year-old junior worker on a farm with six thousand laying hens and three hundred acres of wheat and oilseed. He came to it after his bakery delivery route was cut, lives with his partner Mei, a school office worker, and two children, and has about three weeks of money saved. A pragmatic centrist and occasional AI user, he reads each scenario by which of his tasks it would take. He's calm in the plateau, anxious under steady change, alarmed by two-year AGI, and steadier with more time, planning a move to caretaker work and steering his daughter towards hands-on people work. He's determined not to just hope this time.
biggestWorry: AGI within two years, because both the farm work and his old driving work would vanish, leaving nothing to step onto.
whatWouldHelp: Support that doesn't make people feel like beggars, and local jobs involving people, such as care, schools and maintenance, kept going on purpose.
